claims.text: Controlled decomposition of fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti into a dual-phase microstructure can produce coercivity above 100 Oe.
The matrix in the proposed dual-phase Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy will remain ferromagnetic and fcc.
The secondary phase will be a Ti-rich, magnetically hard L12 or B2 ordered phase.
Ordered secondary-phase precipitates act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Ti addition lowers the stacking-fault energy of the Fe-Co-Ni-Ti matrix.
Ti addition promotes nucleation of ordered L12 or B2 precipitates without destabilizing the fcc matrix.
The secondary phase must have a higher magnetic anisotropy constant than the matrix to provide sufficient pinning force.
A single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti solid solution containing 5–15 at.% Ti has enough Ti to drive subsequent phase separation.
Solution annealing near 1100 °C will establish a homogeneous single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti state.
Aging at 600–800 °C will precipitate a Ti-rich L12 or B2 ordered phase within the fcc matrix.
The fcc matrix Curie temperature is above the proposed 300–500 K operating range.
Nanometer-scale ordered precipitates will create local strain fields in the fcc matrix.
Magnetic-anisotropy mismatch and the physical barrier presented by the precipitates will impede domain-wall motion.
Precipitate-mediated domain-wall pinning will overcome the low coercivity associated with orbital-moment suppression in single-phase fcc alloys.
The aged dual-phase alloy will have a coercive field of 110–150 Oe.
The unaged single-phase fcc baseline will have coercivity below 50 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization because the Ti-rich precipitates are non-magnetic or weakly magnetic.
Low baseline coercivity is caused by suppressed orbital moment and the absence of domain-wall pinning sites.
The coercivity enhancement requires coherent or semi-coherent precipitates that do not form a continuous network disrupting ferromagnetic connectivity.
Excessive Ti can cause a global BCC transformation or large non-magnetic inclusions that degrade magnetic properties.

contradictions.description: The secondary phase is required to be magnetically hard and to possess a higher magnetic anisotropy than the matrix, but it is later described as potentially non-magnetic. A non-magnetic phase cannot supply the proposed intrinsic magnetic-anisotropy contrast, although it could potentially act as a structural pinning obstacle through a different mechanism.
